nodes.name: Multiple points
nodes.statement: In this paper we consider a continuous map $f :M\to N$ between two manifolds and try to find some sufficient conditions for existence of \emph{multiple points}, i.e. the $q$-tuples of pairwise distinct point $x_1,\ldots, x_q\in M$ such that $$ f(x_1) = f(x_2) = \ldots = f(x_q). $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Multiple points of $f$: $q$-tuples of pairwise distinct points of $M$ with the same image.

nodes.name: Coincident q-tuple and multiplicity
nodes.statement: We call such a $q$-tuple $x_1,\ldots, x_q$ a \emph{coincident $q$-tuple}, and call the \emph{multiplicity} of $f$ the maximum $q$ such that there exists a coincident $q$-tuple for $f$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A multiple point $q$-tuple is a coincident $q$-tuple; the multiplicity of $f$ is the largest $q$ admitting one.

nodes.name: Morin canonical form of Sigma^{1^k} singularities
nodes.statement: For example, it is known that a generic (in some sense) smooth map $f:M\to N$ may have singularities of type $\Sigma^{1^k}$, with the following canonical form~\cite{morin1965}. Let the local coordinates be $(x_1,\ldots, x_m)$ in $M$ and $(y_1,\ldots, y_n)$ in $N$. Then the map is given by \begin{eqnarray} y_i &=& x_i,\ i=1,\ldots, m-1\\ y_i &=& \sum_{l=1}^k x_{(i-m)k + l} x_m^l,\ i=m,\ldots, n-1\\ y_n &=& \sum_{l=1}^{k-1} x_{(n-m)k + l} x_m^l + x_m^{k+1}, \end{eqnarray} here the inequality $k(n-m+1)\le m$ must hold.
nodes.section: 2 Local multiplicity of generic smooth maps -- the approach of singularity theory
assumptions: a generic (in some sense) smooth map $f:M\to N$
Let the local coordinates be $(x_1,\ldots, x_m)$ in $M$ and $(y_1,\ldots, y_n)$ in $N$.
conclusions: may have singularities of type $\Sigma^{1^k}$, with the following canonical form~\cite{morin1965}.
nodes.statement_short: Generic smooth maps can have $\Sigma^{1^k}$ singularities with Morin's polynomial canonical form, provided $k(n-m+1)\le m$.

nodes.name: Morin canonical form equations

nodes.label: pol-mid

nodes.name: Morin singularities give coincident (k+1)-tuples
nodes.statement: If we select the numbers $x_i$ ($i=1,\ldots m-1$) so that the polynomials in $x_m$ in the right part of (\ref{pol-mid}) are zero, and the right part of (\ref{pol-last}) has $k+1$ distinct roots, then we obtain a coincident $(k+1)$-tuple, since the coordinate $x_m$ has $k+1$ possible choices.
nodes.section: 2 Local multiplicity of generic smooth maps -- the approach of singularity theory
nodes.statement_short: Choosing coordinates so the middle polynomials vanish and the last has $k+1$ roots yields a coincident $(k+1)$-tuple.

nodes.name: Porteous classes sigma_{k,m-n} for Sigma^{1^k} singularities
nodes.statement: Such singularities for generic maps are guaranteed by the appropriate characteristic classes of the virtual bundle $f^*TN-TM$. The classes $\sigma_{k, m-n}$ for singularities of type $\Sigma^{1^k}$ in codimension $m-n$ can be expressed in terms of Stiefel-Whitney classes by some recurrent formulas, see~\cite{port1971} for example.
nodes.section: 2 Local multiplicity of generic smooth maps -- the approach of singularity theory
nodes.statement_short: Characteristic classes $\sigma_{k,m-n}$ of $f^*TN-TM$ guarantee $\Sigma^{1^k}$ singularities and are recursive in Stiefel-Whitney classes.

nodes.name: Are s_{q,m-n} special cases of sigma_{q,m-n}?
nodes.statement: In particular, in Section~\ref{coind-char} we introduce a characteristic class $s_{q,m-n}$ that guarantee a coincident $q$-tuple for $q=2^l$, the author does not known whether the classes $s_{q,m-n}$ are a particular case of the classes $\sigma_{q,m-n}$.
nodes.section: 2 Local multiplicity of generic smooth maps -- the approach of singularity theory
nodes.statement_short: Unknown whether the paper's classes $s_{q,m-n}$ are a particular case of Porteous' singularity classes $\sigma_{q,m-n}$.

nodes.name: Configuration space K^q(X)
nodes.statement: For a topological space $X$ denote the \emph{configuration space} $$ K^q(X) = \{(x_1, \ldots, x_q)\in X^q : \forall i,j\ x_i\not= x_j\}. $$
nodes.section: 3 Global multiplicity and configuration spaces

nodes.name: Power map f^q on the configuration space
nodes.statement: For any continuous map $f: M\to N$ denote its power $f^q : K^q(M)\to N^q$ its power restricted to $K^q(M)$.
nodes.section: 3 Global multiplicity and configuration spaces

nodes.name: Global obstruction class s_q(f)
nodes.statement: In the case when $M$ and $N$ are smooth manifolds of dimensions $m$ and $n$ respectively, and $M$ is compact, this preimage of the diagonal can be considered as an $\Sigma_q$-equivariant cohomology class $$ s_q(f)\in H_{\Sigma_q}^{n(q-1)}(K^q(M)) = H^{n(q-1)}(K^q(M)/{\Sigma_q}), $$ the coefficients of the cohomology being $Z_2$, or $\mathbb Z$, possibly with the sign action of the group $\Sigma_q$ depending on the orientability of $N$ and parity of its dimension.
nodes.section: 3 Global multiplicity and configuration spaces
nodes.statement_short: For compact $M$, the preimage of the diagonal under $f^q$ defines an equivariant class $s_q(f)\in H^{n(q-1)}(K^q(M)/\Sigma_q)$.

nodes.name: Local multiple points
nodes.statement: This approach would give multiple points, that are close enough to each other in $M$. We call such multiple points \emph{local}.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle

nodes.name: Local multiplicity here is stronger than in the smooth generic case
nodes.statement: Note that this type of local multiplicity is stronger than the local multiplicity in the smooth generic case (see Section~\ref{generic-smooth}), because here we may guarantee the existence of a coincident $q$-tuple $\{x_1,\ldots, x_q\}$ with some small but bounded from below diameter, the bound depending on $M$ only. In will be clear from the definition of $Q^q(M,\ldots)$ in Section~\ref{coind-char}.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: The method yields coincident tuples of diameter bounded below by a constant depending only on $M$.

nodes.name: Injectivity radius r(M)
nodes.statement: Suppose $M$ is a compact Riemannian manifold, and $N$ is a Riemannian manifold with the injectivity radius $r(M)$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle

nodes.name: Exponential map exp: TM -> M x M
nodes.statement: Consider the tangent bundle $TM$ and the exponential map $\exp :TM\to M\times M$, induced by the Riemannian metric, and sending a tangent vector $\tau$ at $x$ to the ends of a geodesic $(x, y)$ with length $|\tau|$ and starting direction $\tau$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle

nodes.name: Construction of exp^q on configurations of short tangent vectors
nodes.statement: Let us fix some $x\in M$, then the $q$-th power $\exp^q : K^q(T_xM) \to M^q$ maps $q$-tuples $(\tau_1,\ldots, \tau_q)\in (T_xM)^q$ of vectors with lengths $<r(M)$ to $q$-tuples of distinct points in $M$. Hence by replacing $T_xM$ with an open disc $D_xM$ of radius $r(M)$ we obtain a well-defined map $\exp^q : K^q(D_xM)\to K^q(M)$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Directly: vectors shorter than the injectivity radius exponentiate to distinct points, so $\exp^q$ is defined fiberwise on disc bundles.

nodes.name: Equivariant map exp^q: K_M^q(DM) -> K^q(M)
nodes.statement: Hence there exists $\Sigma_q$-equivariant map $$ \exp^q : K_M^q(DM) \to K^q(M), $$ here we assume the following definition.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
conclusions: there exists $\Sigma_q$-equivariant map $$ \exp^q : K_M^q(DM) \to K^q(M), $$

nodes.name: Configuration space bundle K_M^q(xi)
nodes.statement: Let $\xi : E(\xi)\to M$ be a vector or disc bundle over $M$. The subspace of $K^q(E(\xi))$, consisting of configurations lying in the same fiber of $\xi$, is denoted $K_M^q(\xi)$ and called the \emph{configuration space bundle}.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
differentia: configurations lying in the same fiber of $\xi$

nodes.name: Reduction of local multiplicity to a fiberwise map
nodes.statement: Now let us consider a continuous map $f :M\to N$. Let us take small enough tangent disc bundle $DN$ so that $\exp$ (of $N$) is invertible on it. Then take small enough tangent disc bundle $DM$ so that the inclusion for the map of pairs $f^2\circ\exp_M DM\subset \exp_N DN$ holds. Then a fiberwise map $$ \phi = \exp_N^{-1}\circ f^2\circ \exp_M : DM\to DN $$ is defined. To find a local coincident $q$-tuple it is sufficient to find a coincident $q$-tuple of the fiberwise map $\phi^q : K_M^q(DM)\to DN^{\oplus q}$, the latter is the $q$-fold Whitney sum of bundles over $N$. Consider the pullback $f^*(DN)$ with the natural fiberwise map $f_* : f^*(DN)\to DN$. Note, that there exists a natural fiberwise map $\psi : DM\to f^*(DN)$, and the corresponding map $\psi^q : K_M^q(DM) \to (f^*(DN))^{\oplus q}$ such that $\phi^q = f_* \circ \psi^q$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate $f$ by exponential maps to get a fiberwise map $\phi$ of tangent disc bundles, and factor it through the pullback $f^*(DN)$.

nodes.name: Local multiplicity bounded by multiplicity of fiberwise map psi
nodes.statement: So the local multiplicity is bounded from below if we bound from below a multiplicity in the fiberwise map $$ \psi : DM \to f^*(DN) $$ over the same space $M$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
conclusions: the local multiplicity is bounded from below if we bound from below a multiplicity in the fiberwise map $$ \psi : DM \to f^*(DN) $$ over the same space $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Local multiple points of $f$ follow from multiple points of the fiberwise map $\psi:DM\to f^*(DN)$ over $M$.

nodes.name: Multiple points of a fiberwise map of vector bundles
nodes.statement: Let us generalize a problem to finding multiple points for a fiberwise map $\psi : \xi\to \eta$ of some vector bundles $\xi$ and $\eta$ over the same space $M$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle

nodes.name: Representation A_q of Sigma_q
nodes.statement: Let $A_q$ be the $q-1$-dimensional representation of $\Sigma_q$, arising from the natural permutation representation on $\mathbb R^q$ by taking the quotient $\mathbb R^q/(1,1,\ldots,1)$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
differentia: arising from the natural permutation representation on $\mathbb R^q$ by taking the quotient $\mathbb R^q/(1,1,\ldots,1)$

nodes.name: Projection xi^q of the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement: Denote the natural projection of the configuration space bundle $\xi^q : K_M^q(\xi)\to M$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle

nodes.name: Coincident tuples as zeros of an equivariant section
nodes.statement: Now the map $\psi^q$ gives an $\Sigma_q$-equivariant section of the vector bundle $(\xi^q)^*(\eta^{\oplus q})$. Composed with the natural projection $$ (\xi^q)^*(\eta^{\oplus q})\to A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta), $$ it also gives a section $\psi_0^q$ of the vector bundle $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$ over $K_M^q(\xi)$. Note that $\psi_0^q$ is an equivariant section w.r.t the natural action of $\Sigma_q$ on $K_M^q(\xi)$ and on $A_q$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Project the section $\psi^q$ of $(\xi^q)^*(\eta^{\oplus q})$ onto $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$ to get an equivariant section $\psi_0^q$.

nodes.name: Reduction to nonempty zero set of equivariant section
nodes.statement: Now the coincident $q$-tuples correspond to the zero set of the section $\psi_0^q$, and we have reduced the problem of finding local multiple points to proving that the zero set of the $\Sigma_q$-equivariant vector bundle $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$ over $K_M^q(\xi)$ is nonempty.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
conclusions: the coincident $q$-tuples correspond to the zero set of the section $\psi_0^q$
nodes.statement_short: Coincident $q$-tuples are zeros of the equivariant section $\psi_0^q$ of $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$ over $K_M^q(\xi)$.

nodes.name: Zero set Z(psi^q, xi, eta)
nodes.statement: Now let us consider the zero set $Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta)$ of some $\Sigma_q$-equivariant section of the bundle $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$ over $K_M^q(\xi)$.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points

nodes.name: Notation A_q tensor eta
nodes.statement: We shall denote the bundle simply $A_q\otimes \eta$ since it does not lead to a confusion.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points

nodes.name: Zero set is Poincare dual to the Euler class
nodes.statement: Certainly, the set $Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta)$ may be considered a manifold for generic sections, and it is Poincare dual to the Euler class $e(A_q\otimes \eta)$, taken in the equivariatn cohomology or some bordism theory. It can be calculated directly sometimes, but we are going to ``stabilize'' it in some sense to simplify the computation, though some information can be lost.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
nodes.statement_short: For generic sections the zero set is a manifold Poincare dual to $e(A_q\otimes\eta)$; the paper will stabilize it.

nodes.name: Identity fiberwise map iota of an auxiliary bundle zeta
nodes.statement: Consider some other vector bundle $\zeta$ and two fiberwise maps $\psi : \xi\to \eta$ and $\iota : \zeta\to\zeta$, the latter being the identity.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points

nodes.name: Stability of coincidence sets under adding identity
nodes.statement: Z((\psi\oplus\iota)^q, \xi\oplus\zeta, \eta\oplus\zeta) = Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta)\times_M \zeta.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
nodes.label: coinc-stability

nodes.name: Nonzero stabilized Euler class forces coincidences
nodes.statement: Hence if the Euler class $e(A_q\otimes(\eta\oplus\zeta))$ is nonzero over $K_M^q(\xi\oplus\zeta)$, then the set $Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta)$ cannot be empty.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
assumptions: the Euler class $e(A_q\otimes(\eta\oplus\zeta))$ is nonzero over $K_M^q(\xi\oplus\zeta)$
conclusions: the set $Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta)$ cannot be empty

nodes.name: Reduction to trivial bundle (Euler class over K^q(R^mu) x M)
nodes.statement: The coincident $q$-tuples in a continuous fiberwise map $\psi : \xi\to\eta$ over $M$ are guaranteed by a nonzero $\Sigma_q$-equivariant Euler class $e(A_q\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))$ in the cohomology (or cobordism) of $K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M$, where $\mu=\dim \xi + \dim \xi^\perp$.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
assumptions: a continuous fiberwise map $\psi : \xi\to\eta$ over $M$
$\mu=\dim \xi + \dim \xi^\perp$
conclusions: are guaranteed by a nonzero $\Sigma_q$-equivariant Euler class $e(A_q\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))$ in the cohomology (or cobordism) of $K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M$
nodes.statement_short: Coincident $q$-tuples of $\psi:\xi\to\eta$ follow from nonvanishing of $e(A_q\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))$ on $K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M$.
nodes.label: triv-reduction

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: In the above reasoning take $\zeta$ to be $\xi^\perp$ such that $\xi\oplus\xi^\perp = \varepsilon^\mu$, $\varepsilon$ denotes a trivial vector bundle. Then it suffices to note that $$ K_M^q(\varepsilon^\mu) = K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M. $$
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
nodes.statement_short: Stabilize with $\zeta=\xi^\perp$ so that $\xi\oplus\xi^\perp$ is trivial and $K_M^q(\varepsilon^\mu)=K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M$.

nodes.name: Kunneth decomposition of equivariant cohomology of K^q(R^mu) x M
nodes.statement: If we consider the cohomology with coefficients in a field $Z_p$, then by the K\"unneth formula the algebra $H_{\Sigma_q}^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M)$ is a free $H^*(M)$-module, spanned by the linear basis of $H^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/{\Sigma_q})$.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
assumptions: we consider the cohomology with coefficients in a field $Z_p$
conclusions: the algebra $H_{\Sigma_q}^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)\times M)$ is a free $H^*(M)$-module, spanned by the linear basis of $H^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/{\Sigma_q})$

nodes.name: Basis h_i of H^*(K^q(R^mu)/Sigma_q)
nodes.statement: Denote the latter basis by $(h_1,\ldots, h_{N(q,\mu)})$, it is known (see~\cite{fuks1970,vass1994,rot2008}) that in the case $p=2$ the elements $h_i$ can be selected to be part of the basis of $H^*(B\Sigma_q, Z_2)$.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points

nodes.name: Characteristic classes s_i from the Euler class decomposition
nodes.statement: Now we can decompose the Euler class $$ e(A_q\otimes (\xi^\perp\oplus\eta)) = \sum_{i=1}^{N(q,\mu)} s_ih_i $$ and obtain the elements $s_i\in H^*(M, Z_p)$, that depend naturally on the bundle $\xi^\perp\oplus\eta$.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
nodes.statement_short: The classes $s_i\in H^*(M,Z_p)$ are the coefficients of $e(A_q\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))$ in the basis $h_i$.

nodes.name: s_i depend only on characteristic classes of eta - xi
nodes.statement: Hence $s_i$ only depend on the Stiefel-Whitney (in case $p=2$) or the Pontryagin and Euler (in case $p$ odd) classes of the virtual bundle $\eta-\xi$, since it is sufficient to consider the situation over some Grassmann variety and then use the naturality of construction.
nodes.section: 5 The Euler class of local multiple points
conclusions: $s_i$ only depend on the Stiefel-Whitney (in case $p=2$) or the Pontryagin and Euler (in case $p$ odd) classes of the virtual bundle $\eta-\xi$
nodes.statement_short: The $s_i$ are characteristic classes of the virtual bundle $\eta-\xi$ (Stiefel-Whitney mod 2, Pontryagin/Euler mod odd $p$).

nodes.name: Top cohomology of K^q(R^mu)/Sigma_q for prime powers q
nodes.statement: Let us consider the case when $q$ is a power of a prime $p$. In this case the cohomology $H^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/{\Sigma_q}, A)$ is zero in dimensions $>(q-1)(\mu-1)$, and its $(q-1)(\mu-1)$-dimensional cohomology is generated by the class $e(A_q)^{n-1}$, see~\cite{vass1988,ossa1996,rot2008,kar2009} for different cases of these results. Here the coefficients $A$ are $Z_p$ for $p=2$ or odd $\mu$, and $Z_p$ with sign action of $\Sigma_q$ in other cases.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
assumptions: the case when $q$ is a power of a prime $p$
conclusions: the cohomology $H^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/{\Sigma_q}, A)$ is zero in dimensions $>(q-1)(\mu-1)$
its $(q-1)(\mu-1)$-dimensional cohomology is generated by the class $e(A_q)^{n-1}$
nodes.statement_short: For prime-power $q$, $H^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/\Sigma_q)$ vanishes above degree $(q-1)(\mu-1)$ and is generated there by a power of $e(A_q)$.

nodes.name: Class s_{q,d} as leading coefficient of the Euler class
nodes.statement: Thus similar to the above definition, we can put $$ e(A_q\otimes (\xi^\perp\oplus\eta)) = s_{q, d}(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta) e(A_q)^{\mu-1} +\ldots, $$ where $d=\dim\eta-\dim\xi = \dim(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta) - \mu$ and $\ldots$ denotes the terms with the dimension of the corresponding class in $H^*(M, Z_p)$ larger, then that of $s_{q, d}$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: $s_{q,d}$ is the coefficient of $e(A_q)^{\mu-1}$ in $e(A_q\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))$, with codimension $d=\dim\eta-\dim\xi$.

nodes.name: Leading characteristic class of local coincident q-tuples
nodes.statement: We call $s_{q, d}(\eta-\xi)$ the \emph{leading characteristic class} of local coincident $q$-tuples for prime powers $q$ at codimension $d$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.definiendum: leading characteristic class of local coincident $q$-tuples

nodes.name: Leading class of local coincident 2^k-tuples
nodes.statement: Let $q$ be a power of two. Denote $w_i$ the Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta-\xi$. Then as a polynomial in the Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta-\xi$ $$ s_{q, d}(\eta-\xi) \equiv w_{d+1}^{q-1} \mod w_{d+2}, w_{d+3}, \ldots. $$
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
assumptions: Let $q$ be a power of two.
Denote $w_i$ the Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta-\xi$.
conclusions: as a polynomial in the Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta-\xi$ $$ s_{q, d}(\eta-\xi) \equiv w_{d+1}^{q-1} \mod w_{d+2}, w_{d+3}, \ldots. $$
nodes.statement_short: For $q=2^k$, $s_{q,d}(\eta-\xi)\equiv w_{d+1}^{q-1}$ modulo the higher Stiefel-Whitney classes $w_{d+2},w_{d+3},\ldots$.
nodes.label: 2k-fold-leading

nodes.name: Hung configuration space Q_0^q(R^n, delta_1..delta_k)
nodes.statement: Let $q=2^k$ and consider a sequence $\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k$ of positive integers such that for any $l<k$ $$ \delta_l > \sum_{i=l+1}^k \delta_i. $$ Let $Q_0^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be the configuration, consisting of one point at the origin. Let by induction $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^n, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ be the set of all $q$-point configurations, such that the first $q/2$ points form a configuration of $Q_0^{q/2}(\mathbb R^n, \delta_2, \ldots, \delta_k)$, shifted by a vector $u$ of length $\delta_1$, and the other $q/2$ points form a configuration of $Q_0^{q/2}(\mathbb R^n, \delta_2, \ldots, \delta_k)$, shifted by a vector $-u$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Inductively: $q=2^k$ points formed by two copies of $Q_0^{q/2}$ shifted by $\pm u$ with $|u|=\delta_1$, for rapidly decreasing $\delta_i$.

nodes.name: Distance-midpoint description of Q_0^q
nodes.statement: A configuration in $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^n, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ can also be described inductively as $x_1,\ldots, x_q\in\mathbb R^n$ such that all the distances $\mathrm{dist}(x_{2i-1}, x_{2i}) = 2\delta_k$ and the midpoints of $[x_{2i-1}, x_{2i}]$ form a configuration of $Q_0^{q/2}(\mathbb R^n, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_{k-1})$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Equivalently, consecutive pairs are at distance $2\delta_k$ and their midpoints form a configuration of $Q_0^{q/2}$.
nodes.label: Qq-defn2

nodes.name: Q_0^q is a product of spheres
nodes.statement: Note that $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^n, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ is always a product of $q-1$ spheres of dimension $n-1$, and we shall omit $\delta_i$ in the notation since it does not change the diffeomorphism type of $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
conclusions: $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^n, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ is always a product of $q-1$ spheres of dimension $n-1$

nodes.name: Bundle Q_M^q(xi) of Hung configurations
nodes.statement: Then we can naturally define the space $Q_M^q(\xi)\subset K_M^q(\xi)$ for any vector bundle $\xi : E(\xi)\to M$ as a bundle of corresponding $Q_0^q(\xi^{-1}(x))$ for $x\in M$.

nodes.name: Distance-midpoint definition applies on Riemannian manifolds
nodes.statement: Note that the Definition~\ref{Qq-defn2} (distance and midpoint characterization) can be applied to any Riemannian manifold $M$, if we allow the last center point (configuration $Q_0^1$) be any $x\in M$. The distances should be chosen small enough in order for the midpoint to be unique.

nodes.name: Configuration space Q^q(M, delta_1..delta_k) on a Riemannian manifold
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold. Define $Q^q(M, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)\subset K^q(M)$ for $q=2^k$ inductively as follows. $Q^1(M) = M$. For $q\ge 2$ let $Q^q(M, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ be the set of $q$-tuples $x_1,\ldots, x_q\in M$ such that all the distances $\mathrm{dist}(x_{2i-1}, x_{2i}) = 2\delta_k$ and the midpoints of $[x_{2i-1}, x_{2i}]$ form a configuration of $Q^{q/2}(M, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_{k-1})$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Inductively, $q$-tuples on $M$ whose consecutive pairs are at distance $2\delta_k$ with midpoints forming a $Q^{q/2}$ configuration.

nodes.name: Q^q(M) is a bundle homeomorphic to Q_M^q(TM)
nodes.statement: Let the injectivity radius of $M$ be $r$ and for all $i=1,\ldots, k$ $$ 2\delta_i < r. $$ Then $Q^q(M, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ is a fiber bundle (the bundle map is the last stage midpoint) over $M$, and is naturally homeomorphic to $Q_M^q(TM)$
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
assumptions: Let the injectivity radius of $M$ be $r$ and for all $i=1,\ldots, k$ $$ 2\delta_i < r. $$
conclusions: $Q^q(M, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ is a fiber bundle (the bundle map is the last stage midpoint) over $M$, and is naturally homeomorphic to $Q_M^q(TM)$
nodes.statement_short: If all $2\delta_i$ are below the injectivity radius, $Q^q(M,\delta)$ fibers over $M$ and is homeomorphic to $Q_M^q(TM)$.
nodes.label: metric-Qq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let us prove by induction. For any configuration $(x_1,\ldots, x_q)\in Q^q(M,\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ the midpoints of pairs $[x_1, x_2], [x_2,x_3],\ldots,[x_{q-1}, x_q]$ form a configuration in $Q^{q/2}(M,\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_{k-1})$. Since $2\delta_k<r$, then knowing the midpoint of $[x_1,x_2]$, the possible positions of the points $x_1,x_2$ form a sphere. So $Q^q(M,\ldots)$ is a product-of-spheres bundle over $Q^{q/2}(M,\ldots)$. Moreover, these spheres are spheres of the vector bundles $\pi_i^*(TM)$, where $\pi_i : Q^{q/2}(M,\ldots)\to M$ is the map, assigning to a configuration its $i$-th point. Note that the maps $\pi_i$ are all homotopic to the centerpoint map $\pi :Q^{q/2}(M,\ldots)\to M$ (the homotopy can be obtained by deforming a point $x_{2i-1}$ or $x_{2i}$ to the midpoint of $[x_{2i-1}, x_{2i}]$, and then repeating inductively), hence all the vector bundles are equivalent to $\pi^*(TM)$. Now the proof is completed by applying the inductive assumption.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$: $Q^q$ is a product-of-spheres bundle over $Q^{q/2}$ whose sphere bundles are all equivalent to $\pi^*(TM)$.

nodes.name: Sylow 2-subgroup Sigma^{(2)}_q
nodes.statement: Let $q=2^k$. Denote $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$ the Sylow subgroup of $\Sigma_q$, generated by all permutations of two consecutive blocks $[a2^l + 1, a2^l + 2^{l-1}]$ and $[a2^l + 2^{l-1}+1, (a+1)2^l]$, where $2\le l \le k$ and $0\le a \le 2^{k-l}-2$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
differentia: generated by all permutations of two consecutive blocks

nodes.name: Top equivariant cohomology of Q^q(R^n) generated by e(A_q)^{n-1}
nodes.statement: The manifold $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^n)$ is $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$-invariant. The cohomology $H_{\Sigma^{(2)}_q}^{(q-1)(n-1)}( Q^q(\mathbb R^n), Z_2)$ is generated by the Euler class $e(A_q)^{n-1}$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
conclusions: The manifold $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^n)$ is $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$-invariant.
The cohomology $H_{\Sigma^{(2)}_q}^{(q-1)(n-1)}( Q^q(\mathbb R^n), Z_2)$ is generated by the Euler class $e(A_q)^{n-1}$.
nodes.label: Qq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: The first claim is obvious by definition. Consider the natural projection $\psi : \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^{n-1}$, defined by $$ \psi(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},x_n) = (x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}). $$ For this projection the only configurations in $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)$ that give coincident $q$-tuples are those with all coordinates zero except $x_n$. But such configurations form exactly one orbit of $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$. Since this orbit is Poincare dual to the Euler class $e(A_q)^{n-1}$, which is responsible for coincident $q$-tuples in this case, we see that $e(A_q)^{n-1}$ coincides with the fundamental class of the manifold $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Use the coordinate projection $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{n-1}$: its coincident tuples form one orbit, Poincare dual to $e(A_q)^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Equivariant mod p cohomology unchanged by passing to a Sylow p-subgroup
nodes.statement: In is well-known~\cite{bro1982}, that if we consider the $\Sigma_q$-equivariant cohomology with coefficients $Z_p$, then the cohomology does not change when passing to $p$-Sylow subgroup.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
assumptions: we consider the $\Sigma_q$-equivariant cohomology with coefficients $Z_p$
conclusions: the cohomology does not change when passing to $p$-Sylow subgroup

nodes.name: Geometric definition of s_{q,d} via pushforward
nodes.statement: Denote $\pi : Q_M^q(\xi)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q \to M$ the natural projection. Then $$ s_{q, d}(\eta-\xi) = \pi_!(e(A_q\otimes \pi^*\eta)), $$ i.e. geometrically it is a projection of the set of coincident $q$-tuples in $Q_M^q(\xi)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$ to $M$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: $s_{q,d}$ is the pushforward to $M$ of the Euler class of $A_q\otimes\pi^*\eta$ over $Q_M^q(\xi)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$.

nodes.name: The two definitions of s_{q,d} agree
nodes.statement: This definition is the same because for the restricted set of coincident $q$-tuples $Z(\psi, \xi, eta)\subseteq Q^q$ of a fiberwise map $\psi : \xi\to \eta$ the stability holds in the following exact form \begin{equation} Z((\psi\oplus\iota)^q, \xi\oplus\zeta, \eta\oplus\zeta) = Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta). \end{equation} Then passing to the case of trivial $\xi$ we see that the topmost cohomology of $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^\mu)$ is the same as in $K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)$. The map $\pi_!$ ``divides'' by the fundamental class of $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$ in $H^*(Q_0^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q\times M)$, similar to the first definition of $s_{q, d}$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Exact stability of coincidence sets in $Q^q$ and equality of top cohomology of $Q_0^q$ and $K^q$ make the two definitions of $s_{q,d}$ agree.

nodes.name: Exact stability of coincidence sets in Q^q
nodes.statement: Z((\psi\oplus\iota)^q, \xi\oplus\zeta, \eta\oplus\zeta) = Z(\psi^q, \xi, \eta).

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Now we are ready to prove Theorem~\ref{2k-fold-leading} using the geometric definition of $s_{q,d}$. Let us find $s_{q,d}$ for a certain fiberwise map over the Grassmannian $M=G_{n, d+1}$ of linear $n$-subspaces in $\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$. Denote the canonical $n$-dimensional bundle $\gamma : E(\gamma)\to G_{n, d+1}$. Now consider the map $$ f :\mathbb R^{n+d+1}\to \mathbb R^{n+d} $$ given by $$ f(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+d+1}) = (x_1 - x_{n+d+1}^2, x_2 - x_{n+d+1}^3,\ldots, x_{n+d} - x_{n+d+1}^{n+d+1}). $$ Each fiber of $\gamma$ is mapped with this map to $\mathbb R^{n+d}$, so $f$ can be considered as a fiberwise map of $\gamma$ to $\varepsilon^{n+d}$. Let us describe the coincident $q$-tuples of $f$ in $Q_M^q(\gamma)$. First, note that there is a natural inclusion $Q_M^q(\gamma)\to Q_0^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1})$. A configuration of $q$ points $(p_1, \ldots, p_q)\in Q_0^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1})$ is mapped to one point $y$ if they lie on a single curve $C(c_1, \ldots, c_{n+d})$, given by the parameterization $$ x_1 = c_1 + t^2,\ x_2 = c_2 + t^3,\ \ldots,\ x_{n+d} = c_{n+d} + t^{n+d+1},\ x_{n+d+1} = t. $$ Consider a single curve $C(c_1,\ldots,c_{n+m})$ and the set $Z(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ of all configurations in $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)$ (not $Q_0^q$!), lying entirely on $C(c_1,\ldots,c_{n+d})$. Consider a configuration $(p_1,\ldots, p_q)\in Z(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ and assume that the points are ordered w.r.t. the coordinate $x_{n+d+1}$, which corresponds with the parameter on the curve. From Definition~\ref{Qq-defn2} it is clear that if $\delta_i$ are small enough in the definition (so that the curvature of $C(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ becomes negligible), then the configuration $(p_1,\ldots, p_q)\in Z(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ is determined uniquely by any one point $p_i$, which can be chosen arbitrarily. In other words, $p_i$ is a smooth parameter on $Z(c_1, \ldots, c_{n+m})/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$. Denote $$ Z=\bigcup_{c_1,\ldots,c_{n+d}\in\mathbb R} Z(c_1, \ldots, c_{n+d})\subset Q^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1}). $$ We have already noted that the map $g_i : Z/\Sigma^{(2)}_q\to\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$ taking any configuration to its $i$-th point w.r.t. the coordinate $x_{n+d+1}$ is a diffeomorphism. For any configuration $(p_1,\ldots, p_q)\in Z$ put $$ h(p_1,\ldots, p_q) = \sum_{i=1}^q g_i(p_1, \ldots, p_q), $$ i.e. the center point of the configuration. The map $h$ is smooth on $Z/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$ and for small enough $\delta_i$ it is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$. Hence $h^{-1}(0)$ is the only configuration in $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1})$ that is mapped into single point by $f$. Since the configuration $h^{-1}(0)$ lies on a translate of the moment curve, which is a convex curve, then its points span some $q-1$-dimensional linear subspace $L\subset\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$. Now any linear space $V\in G_{n, d+1}$, that is supposed to have coincident $q$-tuples in the fiber $Q_0^q(V)$, must contain $L$. Moreover, it can be easily seen that the map $f$ is transversal to zero and the condition $V\supseteq L$ defines the Poincare dual to $s_{q, d}$ homology class. From the well-known description of the (dual) Stiefel-Whitney classes it follows that \begin{equation} s_{q, d} = w_{d+1}^{q-1}(\gamma^\perp) \end{equation} in the cohomology $H^*(G_{n, d+1}, Z_2)$. Now it suffices to note that this cohomology algebra has generators $w_1(\gamma), \ldots, w_n(\gamma)$ and relations \begin{equation} w_{d+2}(\gamma^\perp) = w_{d+3}(\gamma^\perp) = \dots = 0, \end{equation} hence (\ref{dual-sw-power}) holds over arbitrary space modulo higher Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta - \xi$, because the number $n$ can be taken arbitrarily large, and the relations in (\ref{grass-gen}) are the only essential relations.

nodes.statement_short: Universal example over the Grassmannian $G_{n,d+1}$ with a moment-curve map: coincident tuples force $V\supseteq L$, dual to $w_{d+1}^{q-1}(\gamma^\perp)$. Grassmannian relations then give the congruence for arbitrary bundles.

nodes.name: Coincident tuples lie in Q^q(RP^n) for admissible deltas
nodes.statement: Note that this theorem gives a coincident $q$-tuple on a configuration from any subspace $$ Q^q(\mathbb RP^{2^l-2-d}, \delta_1,\ldots, \delta_k)\subset K^q(\mathbb RP^{2^l-2-d}) $$ for any sequence of $\delta_i$, satisfying $$ \delta_1 < \pi/4,\forall i\ \delta_i>\delta_{i+1}+\dots+\delta_k. $$ Here we measure the distance on $\mathbb RP^n$ as the angle between lines.

nodes.statement_short: The coincident $q$-tuple of Theorem 3 can be found in $Q^q(\mathbb RP^{m},\delta)$ for any admissible $\delta_i$ with $\delta_1<\pi/4$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Any map $f : \mathbb RP^m\to \mathbb R^n$ induces a fiberwise map between $\xi=T\mathbb RP^m$ and $\varepsilon^n$. Suppose we have some normal bundle $\xi^\perp$ of dimension $k$. The Stiefel-Whitney class of $\varepsilon^n-\xi$ is $$ w(\varepsilon^n-\xi) = (1+u)^{-m-1} = (1+u)^{2^l-m-1} = (1+u)^{d+1}, $$ and by Theorem~\ref{2k-fold-leading} we have $s_{q,d}(\varepsilon^n-T\mathbb RP^m) = u^{(q-1)(d+1)}$, which is nonzero since $(q-1)(d+1)\le m=2^l-2-d$.

nodes.statement_short: Compute $w(\varepsilon^n-T\mathbb RP^m)=(1+u)^{d+1}$ and apply Theorem 1: $s_{q,d}=u^{(q-1)(d+1)}\neq 0$.

nodes.name: General scheme for computing s_{q,d}
nodes.statement:
Let us give some general schema of calculating $s_{q, d}$ for any particular $q$ and $d$. The class $e(A_q\otimes (\xi^\perp\oplus \eta))$ can be calculated in the assumption that the bundle $\xi^\perp \oplus \eta$ is decomposed into one-dimensional bundles $	au_1,\ldots,	au_
u$ with respective Stiefel-Whitney classes $1+t_1, \ldots, 1 + t_
u$. Let the Stiefel-Whitney class of the representation $A_q$ in the cohomology $H^*(B\Sigma^{(2)}_q, Z_2)$ be $$ e(A_q) = 1 + a_1 + \dots + a_{q-1}. $$ Now the Euler class equals  egin{equation} e(A_q\otimes (	au_1\oplus\dots\oplus	au_
u) ) = \prod_{i=1}^
u (t_i^{q-1} + t_i^{q-2}a_1+\dots + a_{q-1}) \end{equation} in the cohomology $H^*(B\Sigma^{(2)}_q	imes M, Z_2)$. Then we have to map this class to $H^*(K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)	imes M, Z_2)$ or $H^*(Q^q(\mathbb R^\mu)	imes M, Z_2)$, by the natural map $$ K^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/\Sigma_q	o B\Sigma_q,\ 	ext{or}\ Q^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q	o B\Sigma^{(2)}_q, $$ find the coefficient at $a_{q-1}^{\mu-1}$, and express it in the Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta-\xi$. Of course, the knowledge of the cohomology of the symmetric group modulo $2$ and the relations on these cohomology that describe $H^*(Q^q(\mathbb R^\mu)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q)$ should be known.

nodes.name: Computation of s_{4,d} for coincident 4-tuples
nodes.statement:
Passing to the particular case $q=4$ note that $\Sigma^{(2)}_4$ is the square group $D_8$, and its cohomology is multiplicatively generated by three elements $a, b, c$ such that $$ \dim a = \dim c = 1,\quad \dim b = 2, $$ and the relation $ac=0$. The Stiefel-Whitney class of $A_4$ is $$ w(A_4) = (1 + (a+c) + b)(1 + c). $$ The space $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)$ is a product of three $n-1$-spheres, and in the cohomology of $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$ we have relations $$ c^n=b^n=0. $$ Now (ef{euler-formula}) has the form $$ e(A_q\otimes (	au_1\oplus\dots\oplus	au_
u) ) = \prod_{i=1}^
u (t_i^2 + (a+c)t_i+b)(t_i+c). $$ to find the leading characteristic class of coincident $4$-tuples in codimension $d$ we have to find the coefficient at $(bc)^{
u-d-1}$ after applying all the relations. We can also add the artificial relation $a=0$ to simplify the situation, since it does not affect anything. Then some direct calculations give, for example $$ s_{4,0} = w_1^3+w_1w_2, $$ $$ s_{4,1} = w_2^3 + w_3^2 + w_1w_2w_3 + w_2w_4. $$ Further cases can be considered too, it even seems plausible to have some explicit formula with summation for $q=4$.

nodes.name: Reduction to the cyclic Sylow subgroup Z_p for odd p
nodes.statement: Let us consider local coincident $p$-tuples for odd prime $p$. In this case we consider the Euler class $e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta))$ modulo $p$, and therefore we may consider, instead of $\Sigma_p$ its $p$-Sylow subgroup $Z_p$ of cyclic permutations. nodes.name: Euler class of A_p tensor a bundle via splitting principle
nodes.statement:
Similar to (ef{euler-formula}), by the splitting principle we decompose $\xi^\perp\oplus \eta$ of dimension $
u$ into the sum of $k$ two-dimensional oriented (because we do everything $\mod p$) bundles $\sigma_1\oplus\dots\oplus\sigma_k$, when $
u=2k$, or into the sum $\sigma_1\oplus\dots\oplus\sigma_k\oplus	au$ with $\dim	au=1$, when $
u=2k+1$. In either case we have $$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = \prod_{i=1}^k e(A_p\otimes \sigma_i) = \prod_{i=1}^k (u^2-e_i^{p-1}), $$ for even $
u$, and $$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = u\prod_{i=1}^k (u^2-e_i^{p-1}) $$ for odd $
u$. In the last two formulas $u=e(A_p)$, and $e_i=e(\sigma_i)$ are the Euler classes of summands.
nodes.section: 9 Local coincident $p$-tuples for prime $p$
assumptions:
by the splitting principle we decompose $\xi^\perp\oplus \eta$ of dimension $
u$ into the sum of $k$ two-dimensional oriented (because we do everything $\mod p$) bundles $\sigma_1\oplus\dots\oplus\sigma_k$, when $
u=2k$, or into the sum $\sigma_1\oplus\dots\oplus\sigma_k\oplus	au$ with $\dim	au=1$, when $
u=2k+1$
conclusions: $$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = \prod_{i=1}^k e(A_p\otimes \sigma_i) = \prod_{i=1}^k (u^2-e_i^{p-1}), $$ for even $\nu$
$$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = u\prod_{i=1}^k (u^2-e_i^{p-1}) $$ for odd $\nu$
nodes.statement_short: Mod $p$, $e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))=u^{\epsilon}\prod_i(u^2-e_i^{p-1})$ over a splitting into oriented 2-plane bundles.

nodes.name: Justification of the Euler class product formula
nodes.statement: The formula follows from the formula of Pontryagin classes of a tensor product along with the fact that the only nonzero characteristic classes of $A_p$ in $H^*(BZ_p, Z_p)$ are its Euler class $u$ and its topmost Pontryagin class $u^2$.
nodes.section: 9 Local coincident $p$-tuples for prime $p$
nodes.statement_short: Tensor-product formula for Pontryagin classes, using that $A_p$ has only Euler class $u$ and top Pontryagin class $u^2$ mod $p$.

nodes.name: Characteristic classes alpha_{p,i}
nodes.statement: Let us define the following characteristic classes by the splitting principle: if the Pontryagin classes are expressed through symmetric functions $$ p_{4i} = \sigma_i(t_1^2, \ldots, t_k^2) $$ Then put $$ \alpha_{p,i} = \sigma_i(t_1^{p-1}, \ldots, t_k^{p-1}), $$ in the case $p=3$ these are the Pontryagin classes again, in the general case these are some classes of dimension $2(p-1)i$.
nodes.section: 9 Local coincident $p$-tuples for prime $p$
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha_{p,i}$ is the $i$-th elementary symmetric function of $t_j^{p-1}$, where $p_{4i}=\sigma_i(t_j^2)$; for $p=3$ these are Pontryagin classes.

nodes.name: Euler class expansion in alpha_{p,i}
nodes.statement: Now we can rewrite $$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = \sum_{i=0}^k (-1)^i u^{2(k-i)}\alpha_{p,i}(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta) $$ for even $\nu$ and $$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = \sum_{i=0}^k (-1)^i u^{2(k-i)+1}\alpha_{p,i}(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta) $$ for odd $\nu$.
nodes.section: 9 Local coincident $p$-tuples for prime $p$
conclusions: $$ e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta)) = \sum_{i=0}^k (-1)^i u^{2(k-i)}\alpha_{p,i}(\xi^\perp\oplus \eta) $$ for even $\nu$
nodes.statement_short: $e(A_p\otimes(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta))=\sum_i(-1)^i u^{2(k-i)(+1)}\alpha_{p,i}(\xi^\perp\oplus\eta)$.

nodes.name: Argument for Theorem 4
nodes.statement: The images of $u^i$ in $H^{(p-1)i}(K^p(\mathbb R^\mu), Z_p)$ are nonzero if $i \le \mu-1$. Hence we obtain a theorem.
nodes.section: 9 Local coincident $p$-tuples for prime $p$
nodes.statement_short: Powers $u^i$ with $i\le\mu-1$ survive in the configuration space, so the coefficients $\alpha_{p,i}$ of the expansion are obstructions.

nodes.name: Characteristic classes of coincident p-tuples for prime p
nodes.statement: The characteristic classes of coincident $p$-tuples in a fiberwise map $\xi\to\eta$ are the classes $\alpha_{p,i}(\eta-\xi)$ with $2i\ge \dim\eta-\dim\xi + 1$.
nodes.section: 9 Local coincident $p$-tuples for prime $p$
assumptions: a fiberwise map $\xi\to\eta$
$2i\ge \dim\eta-\dim\xi + 1$
conclusions: The characteristic classes of coincident $p$-tuples in a fiberwise map $\xi\to\eta$ are the classes $\alpha_{p,i}(\eta-\xi)$
nodes.label: p-fold-coinc

nodes.name: Same classes bound genus and LS category of configuration spaces
nodes.statement: Note that the same classes give new lower bounds for the Lyusternik-Schnirelmann category of $K^q(M)/\Sigma_q$ and the Krasnosel'skii-Schwarz genus of $K^q(M)$, thus improving the results of~\cite{vass1988,ossa1996,rot2008,kar2009}, where the estimate was made depending on the dimension of $M$ only.
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces

nodes.name: Krasnosel'skii-Schwarz genus g(X)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a free $G$-space, the \emph{genus} of $X$ is the minimal size of $G$-invariant open cover (i.e. cover by $G$-invariant open subsets) $\{X_1,\ldots,X_n\}$ of $X$ such that every $X_i$ can be $G$-mapped to $G$. Denote the genus of $X$ by $g(X)$.
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces

nodes.name: Genus bounds Lyusternik-Schnirelmann category
nodes.statement: It is also well-known that the genus $g(X)$ estimates the Lyusternik-Schnirelmann category $\mathrm{cat} X/G$ from below.
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
conclusions: the genus $g(X)$ estimates the Lyusternik-Schnirelmann category $\mathrm{cat} X/G$ from below

nodes.name: Cohomological lower bound for genus and category
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a paracompact free $G$-space, and for some $G$-module $\alpha$ the natural cohomology map $$ \pi_X^* : H^n(BG, \alpha)\to H_G^n(X, \alpha) $$ is nontrivial, then $$ \mathrm{cat} X/G \ge g(X)\ge n+1. $$
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
assumptions: $X$ is a paracompact free $G$-space
for some $G$-module $\alpha$ the natural cohomology map $$ \pi_X^* : H^n(BG, \alpha)\to H_G^n(X, \alpha) $$ is nontrivial
conclusions: $$ \mathrm{cat} X/G \ge g(X)\ge n+1. $$
nodes.label: gen-by-coh

nodes.name: Genus bound for K^q(M) from powers of e(A_q)
nodes.statement: If the natural image of $e(A_q)^n$ is the cohomology of $K^q(M)$ (or $K_M^q(TM)$) is nontrivial, then $$ \mathrm{cat} K^q(M)/\Sigma_q \ge g(K^q(M))\ge (q-1)n + 1. $$
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
assumptions: the natural image of $e(A_q)^n$ is the cohomology of $K^q(M)$ (or $K_M^q(TM)$) is nontrivial
conclusions: $$ \mathrm{cat} K^q(M)/\Sigma_q \ge g(K^q(M))\ge (q-1)n + 1. $$
nodes.label: gen-by-euler

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Note that we have an $\Sigma_q$-equivariant map $$ \exp : K_M^q(TM)\to K^q(M). $$ If $e(A_q)^n\not=0\in K_M^q(TM)$, then $e(A_q)^n\not=0\in K^q(M)$, and then we apply Lemma~\ref{gen-by-coh}.
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
nodes.statement_short: Push nonvanishing of $e(A_q)^n$ along the equivariant map $\exp:K_M^q(TM)\to K^q(M)$ and apply Lemma 4.

nodes.name: Genus of configuration spaces from dual Stiefel-Whitney classes
nodes.statement: Suppose that the dual Stiefel-Whitney class of $M$ with $\dim M=m$ has the form $$ w(TM^\perp) = 1+\bar w_1+\dots+\bar w_{d+1}, $$ $q$ is a power of two, and $\bar w_{d+1}^{q-1}\not=0$. Then $$ g(K^q(M))\ge (m + d)(q-1) + 1. $$ In particular if $q(d+1) < 2^l-1$ then $$ g(K^q(RP^{2^l-2-d}))\ge (2^l-3)(q-1) + 1. $$
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
assumptions: the dual Stiefel-Whitney class of $M$ with $\dim M=m$ has the form $$ w(TM^\perp) = 1+\bar w_1+\dots+\bar w_{d+1}, $$
$q$ is a power of two
conclusions: In particular if $q(d+1) < 2^l-1$ then $$ g(K^q(RP^{2^l-2-d}))\ge (2^l-3)(q-1) + 1. $$
nodes.statement_short: If $\bar w_{d+1}^{q-1}\ne0$ is the top dual Stiefel-Whitney class, then $g(K^q(M))\ge(m+d)(q-1)+1$; in particular for projective spaces.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5
nodes.statement: Denote the dimension of normal bundle $k=\dim TM^\perp$. Theorem~\ref{2k-fold-leading} claims that the Euler class $$ e(A_q\otimes (TM^\perp\oplus\varepsilon^{m+d}))\in H^{(q-1)(k + m + d)}(K^q(\mathbb R^{m+k})\times M) $$ is nonzero under the assumptions. Lemma~\ref{triv-reduction} now claims that the Euler class $e(A_q\otimes \varepsilon^{m+d})=e(A_q)^{m+d}$ is also nonzero in $K_M^q(TM)$. Now the result follows from Lemma~\ref{gen-by-euler}.
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1 gives a nonzero Euler class; Lemma 1 transfers it to $e(A_q)^{m+d}\ne0$ on $K_M^q(TM)$; Lemma 5 gives the bound.

nodes.name: Genus of K^4(M) from normal Stiefel-Whitney classes
nodes.statement: Denote $\bar w_i$ the Stiefel-whitney classes of the normal bundle $TM^\perp$. If the class $$ \bar w_1^3+\bar w_1\bar w_2 $$ is nonzero on $M$ then $$ g(K^4(M))\ge 3m + 1. $$ If the class $$ \bar w_2^3 + \bar w_3^2 + \bar w_1\bar w_2\bar w_3 + \bar w_2\bar w_4 $$ is nonzero on $M$ then $$ g(K^4(M))\ge 3m + 4. $$
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
assumptions: the class $$ \bar w_1^3+\bar w_1\bar w_2 $$ is nonzero on $M$
the class $$ \bar w_2^3 + \bar w_3^2 + \bar w_1\bar w_2\bar w_3 + \bar w_2\bar w_4 $$ is nonzero on $M$

nodes.name: Genus of K^p(M) from classes alpha_{p,i}
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a prime. Consider the classes $\bar \alpha_{p,i}$ of the normal bundle $TM^\perp$, introduced in Section~\ref{p-fold}. If $\bar \alpha_{p, i}\not=0$ for some $i$, then $$ g(K^p(M))\ge (m + 2i - 1)(p-1) + 1. $$
nodes.section: 10 Estimating the equivariant category of configuration spaces
assumptions: Let $p$ be a prime.
$\bar \alpha_{p, i}\not=0$ for some $i$

nodes.name: Define the fiberwise map $\phi$ between tangent disc bundles
nodes.statement: Now let us consider a continuous map $f :M\to N$. Let us take small enough tangent disc bundle $DN$ so that $\exp$ (of $N$) is invertible on it. Then take small enough tangent disc bundle $DM$ so that the inclusion for the map of pairs $f^2\circ\exp_M DM\subset \exp_N DN$ holds. Then a fiberwise map $$ \phi = \exp_N^{-1}\circ f^2\circ \exp_M : DM\to DN $$ is defined.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Define the fiberwise map $\phi$ between tangent disc bundles

nodes.name: Reduce to coincident tuples of the fiberwise map $\phi^q$
nodes.statement: To find a local coincident $q$-tuple it is sufficient to find a coincident $q$-tuple of the fiberwise map $\phi^q : K_M^q(DM)\to DN^{\oplus q}$, the latter is the $q$-fold Whitney sum of bundles over $N$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to coincident tuples of the fiberwise map $\phi^q$

nodes.name: Factor $\phi^q$ through the pullback via $\psi^q$
nodes.statement: Consider the pullback $f^*(DN)$ with the natural fiberwise map $f_* : f^*(DN)\to DN$. Note, that there exists a natural fiberwise map $\psi : DM\to f^*(DN)$, and the corresponding map $\psi^q : K_M^q(DM) \to (f^*(DN))^{\oplus q}$ such that $\phi^q = f_* \circ \psi^q$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Factor $\phi^q$ through the pullback via $\psi^q$

nodes.name: Build the section $\psi_0^q$ of $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$
nodes.statement: Now the map $\psi^q$ gives an $\Sigma_q$-equivariant section of the vector bundle $(\xi^q)^*(\eta^{\oplus q})$. Composed with the natural projection $$ (\xi^q)^*(\eta^{\oplus q})\to A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta), $$ it also gives a section $\psi_0^q$ of the vector bundle $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$ over $K_M^q(\xi)$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Build the section $\psi_0^q$ of $A_q\otimes(\xi^q)^*(\eta)$

nodes.name: Note the section is equivariant
nodes.statement: Note that $\psi_0^q$ is an equivariant section w.r.t the natural action of $\Sigma_q$ on $K_M^q(\xi)$ and on $A_q$.
nodes.section: 4 Local multiplicity of continuous maps -- the configuration space bundle
nodes.statement_short: Note the section is equivariant

nodes.name: Induction: midpoints form a smaller configuration and the pair positions form a sphere
nodes.statement: Let us prove by induction. For any configuration $(x_1,\ldots, x_q)\in Q^q(M,\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ the midpoints of pairs $[x_1, x_2], [x_2,x_3],\ldots,[x_{q-1}, x_q]$ form a configuration in $Q^{q/2}(M,\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_{k-1})$. Since $2\delta_k<r$, then knowing the midpoint of $[x_1,x_2]$, the possible positions of the points $x_1,x_2$ form a sphere.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Induction: midpoints form a smaller configuration and the pair positions form a sphere

nodes.name: Midpoints of pairs form a $Q^{q/2}$ configuration
nodes.statement: For any configuration $(x_1,\ldots, x_q)\in Q^q(M,\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_k)$ the midpoints of pairs $[x_1, x_2], [x_2,x_3],\ldots,[x_{q-1}, x_q]$ form a configuration in $Q^{q/2}(M,\delta_1, \ldots, \delta_{k-1})$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Midpoints of pairs form a $Q^{q/2}$ configuration

nodes.name: Given the midpoint, the pair ranges over a sphere
nodes.statement: Since $2\delta_k<r$, then knowing the midpoint of $[x_1,x_2]$, the possible positions of the points $x_1,x_2$ form a sphere.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Given the midpoint, the pair ranges over a sphere

nodes.name: $Q^q$ is a product-of-spheres bundle over $Q^{q/2}$
nodes.statement: So $Q^q(M,\ldots)$ is a product-of-spheres bundle over $Q^{q/2}(M,\ldots)$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: $Q^q$ is a product-of-spheres bundle over $Q^{q/2}$

nodes.name: Identify the spheres as spheres of $\pi_i^*(TM)$
nodes.statement: Moreover, these spheres are spheres of the vector bundles $\pi_i^*(TM)$, where $\pi_i : Q^{q/2}(M,\ldots)\to M$ is the map, assigning to a configuration its $i$-th point.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Identify the spheres as spheres of $\pi_i^*(TM)$

nodes.name: All $\pi_i$ are homotopic to the center map; conclude by induction
nodes.statement: Note that the maps $\pi_i$ are all homotopic to the centerpoint map $\pi :Q^{q/2}(M,\ldots)\to M$ (the homotopy can be obtained by deforming a point $x_{2i-1}$ or $x_{2i}$ to the midpoint of $[x_{2i-1}, x_{2i}]$, and then repeating inductively), hence all the vector bundles are equivalent to $\pi^*(TM)$. Now the proof is completed by applying the inductive assumption.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: All $\pi_i$ are homotopic to the center map; conclude by induction

nodes.name: Invariance is immediate; introduce the coordinate projection $\psi$
nodes.statement: The first claim is obvious by definition. Consider the natural projection $\psi : \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^{n-1}$, defined by $$ \psi(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},x_n) = (x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}). $$
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Invariance is immediate; introduce the coordinate projection $\psi$

nodes.name: Coincident tuples of $\psi$ form one $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$-orbit
nodes.statement: For this projection the only configurations in $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)$ that give coincident $q$-tuples are those with all coordinates zero except $x_n$. But such configurations form exactly one orbit of $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: Coincident tuples of $\psi$ form one $\Sigma^{(2)}_q$-orbit

nodes.name: The orbit is Poincare dual to $e(A_q)^{n-1}$, the fundamental class
nodes.statement: Since this orbit is Poincare dual to the Euler class $e(A_q)^{n-1}$, which is responsible for coincident $q$-tuples in this case, we see that $e(A_q)^{n-1}$ coincides with the fundamental class of the manifold $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$.
nodes.section: 6 Local coincident $p^k$-tuples and their characteristic classes
nodes.statement_short: The orbit is Poincare dual to $e(A_q)^{n-1}$, the fundamental class

nodes.name: Use the geometric definition of $s_{q,d}$
nodes.statement: Now we are ready to prove Theorem~\ref{2k-fold-leading} using the geometric definition of $s_{q,d}$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Use the geometric definition of $s_{q,d}$

nodes.name: Universal example: map $f$ on the canonical bundle over $G_{n,d+1}$
nodes.statement: Let us find $s_{q,d}$ for a certain fiberwise map over the Grassmannian $M=G_{n, d+1}$ of linear $n$-subspaces in $\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$. Denote the canonical $n$-dimensional bundle $\gamma : E(\gamma)\to G_{n, d+1}$. Now consider the map $$ f :\mathbb R^{n+d+1}\to \mathbb R^{n+d} $$ given by $$ f(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+d+1}) = (x_1 - x_{n+d+1}^2, x_2 - x_{n+d+1}^3,\ldots, x_{n+d} - x_{n+d+1}^{n+d+1}). $$ Each fiber of $\gamma$ is mapped with this map to $\mathbb R^{n+d}$, so $f$ can be considered as a fiberwise map of $\gamma$ to $\varepsilon^{n+d}$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Universal example: map $f$ on the canonical bundle over $G_{n,d+1}$

nodes.name: Coincident tuples lie on curves $C(c_1,\ldots,c_{n+d})$
nodes.statement: Let us describe the coincident $q$-tuples of $f$ in $Q_M^q(\gamma)$. First, note that there is a natural inclusion $Q_M^q(\gamma)\to Q_0^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1})$. A configuration of $q$ points $(p_1, \ldots, p_q)\in Q_0^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1})$ is mapped to one point $y$ if they lie on a single curve $C(c_1, \ldots, c_{n+d})$, given by the parameterization $$ x_1 = c_1 + t^2,\ x_2 = c_2 + t^3,\ \ldots,\ x_{n+d} = c_{n+d} + t^{n+d+1},\ x_{n+d+1} = t. $$
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Coincident tuples lie on curves $C(c_1,\ldots,c_{n+d})$

nodes.name: By Definition 5, a configuration on a curve is determined by one point
nodes.statement: Consider a single curve $C(c_1,\ldots,c_{n+m})$ and the set $Z(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ of all configurations in $Q^q(\mathbb R^n)$ (not $Q_0^q$!), lying entirely on $C(c_1,\ldots,c_{n+d})$. Consider a configuration $(p_1,\ldots, p_q)\in Z(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ and assume that the points are ordered w.r.t. the coordinate $x_{n+d+1}$, which corresponds with the parameter on the curve. From Definition~\ref{Qq-defn2} it is clear that if $\delta_i$ are small enough in the definition (so that the curvature of $C(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ becomes negligible), then the configuration $(p_1,\ldots, p_q)\in Z(c_1,\ldots, c_{n+m})$ is determined uniquely by any one point $p_i$, which can be chosen arbitrarily. In other words, $p_i$ is a smooth parameter on $Z(c_1, \ldots, c_{n+m})/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: By Definition 5, a configuration on a curve is determined by one point

nodes.name: Introduce $Z$ and the point maps $g_i$
nodes.statement: Denote $$ Z=\bigcup_{c_1,\ldots,c_{n+d}\in\mathbb R} Z(c_1, \ldots, c_{n+d})\subset Q^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1}). $$ We have already noted that the map $g_i : Z/\Sigma^{(2)}_q\to\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$ taking any configuration to its $i$-th point w.r.t. the coordinate $x_{n+d+1}$ is a diffeomorphism.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $Z$ and the point maps $g_i$

nodes.name: Center map $h$ is a diffeomorphism, so exactly one centered configuration coincides
nodes.statement: For any configuration $(p_1,\ldots, p_q)\in Z$ put $$ h(p_1,\ldots, p_q) = \sum_{i=1}^q g_i(p_1, \ldots, p_q), $$ i.e. the center point of the configuration. The map $h$ is smooth on $Z/\Sigma^{(2)}_q$ and for small enough $\delta_i$ it is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$. Hence $h^{-1}(0)$ is the only configuration in $Q_0^q(\mathbb R^{n+d+1})$ that is mapped into single point by $f$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Center map $h$ is a diffeomorphism, so exactly one centered configuration coincides

nodes.name: Coincidences in $V$ require $V\supseteq L$, which is Poincare dual to $s_{q,d}$
nodes.statement: Since the configuration $h^{-1}(0)$ lies on a translate of the moment curve, which is a convex curve, then its points span some $q-1$-dimensional linear subspace $L\subset\mathbb R^{n+d+1}$. Now any linear space $V\in G_{n, d+1}$, that is supposed to have coincident $q$-tuples in the fiber $Q_0^q(V)$, must contain $L$. Moreover, it can be easily seen that the map $f$ is transversal to zero and the condition $V\supseteq L$ defines the Poincare dual to $s_{q, d}$ homology class.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Coincidences in $V$ require $V\supseteq L$, which is Poincare dual to $s_{q,d}$

nodes.name: Schubert-cycle description gives $s_{q,d}=w_{d+1}^{q-1}(\gamma^\perp)$
nodes.statement: From the well-known description of the (dual) Stiefel-Whitney classes it follows that \begin{equation} s_{q, d} = w_{d+1}^{q-1}(\gamma^\perp) \end{equation} in the cohomology $H^*(G_{n, d+1}, Z_2)$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Schubert-cycle description gives $s_{q,d}=w_{d+1}^{q-1}(\gamma^\perp)$

nodes.name: Grassmannian relations are the only ones, so the formula holds universally mod higher classes
nodes.statement: Now it suffices to note that this cohomology algebra has generators $w_1(\gamma), \ldots, w_n(\gamma)$ and relations \begin{equation} w_{d+2}(\gamma^\perp) = w_{d+3}(\gamma^\perp) = \dots = 0, \end{equation} hence (\ref{dual-sw-power}) holds over arbitrary space modulo higher Stiefel-Whitney classes of $\eta - \xi$, because the number $n$ can be taken arbitrarily large, and the relations in (\ref{grass-gen}) are the only essential relations.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Grassmannian relations are the only ones, so the formula holds universally mod higher classes

nodes.name: Reduce to a fiberwise map $T\mathbb RP^m\to\varepsilon^n$
nodes.statement: Any map $f : \mathbb RP^m\to \mathbb R^n$ induces a fiberwise map between $\xi=T\mathbb RP^m$ and $\varepsilon^n$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a fiberwise map $T\mathbb RP^m\to\varepsilon^n$

nodes.name: Compute $w(\varepsilon^n-\xi)=(1+u)^{d+1}$ and apply Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Suppose we have some normal bundle $\xi^\perp$ of dimension $k$. The Stiefel-Whitney class of $\varepsilon^n-\xi$ is $$ w(\varepsilon^n-\xi) = (1+u)^{-m-1} = (1+u)^{2^l-m-1} = (1+u)^{d+1}, $$ and by Theorem~\ref{2k-fold-leading} we have $s_{q,d}(\varepsilon^n-T\mathbb RP^m) = u^{(q-1)(d+1)}$, which is nonzero since $(q-1)(d+1)\le m=2^l-2-d$.
nodes.section: 7 Proof of Theorem~1 and some corollaries

nodes.name: Theorem 1 gives a nonzero Euler class
